title: When Investors Say They Don't Back Solo Founders, It's Usually Just a Polite No
dek: 65% of startups die from people problems, and in an early-stage company the only "people" are the co-founders — so "we don't back solo founders" is often just the easiest exit for an investor who doesn't want to tell the truth.
why: Medium information density, but two judgments — the denominator delusion and the idea that a pass is a face-saving excuse — can directly change how you handle your own fundraise.
who: Founders who are considering going solo or have already been rejected by investors with "we don't back solo founders," and early-stage investors who want to understand what actually kills early-stage companies.
skip: 07:08 to 08:09 is a recruitment ad for the solo founder program; you can skip it.

points.h: A co-founder isn't table stakes, it's a high bar
points.body: They've spent seven years helping people find co-founders, and they still believe an excellent co-founder is enormously valuable — but the bar should be absurdly high. Don't force a convenience co-founder just because "people think you should have one." Their position isn't "don't find a co-founder," it's "don't let the search for a co-founder stop you from starting."

points.h: Companies die from people problems, and early on the only person is the founder
points.body: About 65% of companies fail because of people problems, not product or customers. And when a company is just getting started, the only "person" in it is the co-founder — so the co-founder is itself the leading source of company death. That leads directly to a counterintuitive conclusion: a solo founder actually sidesteps the biggest cause of early-stage death.

points.h: The number one killer of solo founders is loneliness
points.body: Solo founders have no co-founder, so the most common early-stage blowup cause doesn't apply to them; their real failure point is loneliness. With no teammate, no one with equal stake and equal incentive to carry it with them, things hit extremely hard when they go wrong. Their solution isn't to force you into a pair — it's to build solo together: gather solo founders each building their own company, giving each other context, connections and insight, without forcing anyone into a team.

points.h: Not backing solo founders is the easiest rejection line
points.body: Investors really do have a bias against solo founders, but more often it's just the least offensive reason to say no. Saying "I'd love to back you, but I don't back solo founders" is far easier than saying "I don't believe in you, your company, or your market." So don't take a pass too seriously, and don't expect them to change their minds — they usually won't. But equally, don't over-read the reason for the pass: unless they gave you very direct, very brutal feedback, it's mostly just relationship maintenance.

points.h: With no co-founder, investors can only read your hiring
points.body: Investors will care especially about who you hire next, because without a co-founder they've lost the ready-made yardstick for judging your talent bar. Every person you hire adds a cultural signal to the company: you're founder and CEO, but after three hires, 75% of the people aren't founders. So investors want to know what your talent standard is. The exception is a company like Pulseia's Ben, pursuing true solo and hiring as few people as possible.

points.h: Solo founders don't have to optimize only for valuation
points.body: If the company is split three ways, dilution hurts much more, so you might accept a higher valuation from a lower-quality firm just to dilute less. Solo founders don't have that pressure and can prioritize a firm with a better reputation, one more likely to help you than hurt you. The conclusion: valuation is just one of many variables when choosing a lead investor, and it shouldn't be the only one.

points.h: The denominator delusion: failed companies had co-founders too
points.body: The data argument against solo founders is that "most of the most successful companies were co-founded" — which is true as far as it goes. But it's missing the denominator: how many failed companies were also co-founded? Once you count the denominator, you find that far more co-founded companies fail. The denominator is so large for two reasons: everyone thinks you must have a co-founder, and co-founders are precisely why most companies die. Solo founders have a smaller numerator and a smaller denominator; you still have a chance to be a winner, you just have to keep going.

points.h: People who worry they have solo founder syndrome usually don't
points.body: Solo founder syndrome is roughly understood as "can't work well with others." Their retort: then what syndrome do the 65% of companies that break up over co-founders have? There really are people who want a co-founder but can't find one because they're a jerk, but the people who worry "am I a jerk?" are exactly the ones who don't need to worry — the ones who should worry would never let the thought enter their heads.
